questiontext.text:
Use the idea of Euclid's proof to show that there are infinitely many primes of the form \(6k + 5\): primes that leave remainder 5 on division by 6, such as 5, 11, 17 and 23.

Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many, \(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n\), and let \(P = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n\) be their product. You may use this fact: every integer greater than 1 that leaves remainder 5 on division by 6 has at least one prime factor that leaves remainder 5 on division by 6.

  1. Give an example of a number \(M\), in terms of \(P\), that the proof can use in place of Euclid's \(N\).

    \(M =\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

  2. A student suggests \(M = 6P + 5\). Why does this not work?

    [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Take \(M = 6P - 1 = 6p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n - 1\). It is greater than 1, and it leaves remainder 5 on division by 6, since \(6P - 1 = 6(P - 1) + 5\). So, by the fact given, \(M\) has a prime factor \(q\) of the form \(6k + 5\). But dividing \(M\) by any \(p_i\) leaves remainder \(p_i - 1\), so \(q\) is not one of \(p_1, \ldots, p_n\). This contradicts the assumption that the list contains all such primes.

Other choices work too, such as \(12P - 1\) or \(6P - 7\). What matters is that \(M \gt 1\), that \(M\) leaves remainder 5 on division by 6, and that no \(p_i\) divides \(M\). Euclid's \(P + 1\) fails the second condition: if the list were 5 and 11, then \(P + 1 = 56 = 2^3 \times 7\), with no prime factor of the form \(6k + 5\). The student's \(6P + 5\) fails the third, because 5 is in the list and divides it.

Why the fact holds: a number of the form \(6k + 5\) is odd and not a multiple of 3, so each of its prime factors leaves remainder 1 or 5 on division by 6. A product of numbers that all leave remainder 1 leaves remainder 1, so at least one factor leaves remainder 5.

questionnote.text: Fixed: (a) any M such as 6P - 1; (b) w_five

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 8.2 (Solution 8.2, p. 38) in Section 8 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022: its method is applied to primes of the form 6k + 5.

node.description: M has all three properties on every test list

truefeedback.text: Yes. Your \(M\) is greater than 1, leaves remainder 5 on division by 6, and none of \(p_1, \ldots, p_n\) divides it. So it has a prime factor of the form \(6k + 5\) that is not in the list: a contradiction.

That is Euclid's \(N\). None of \(p_1, \ldots, p_n\) divides it, but it need not have a prime factor of the form \(6k + 5\): if the list were 5 and 11, then \(P + 1 = 56 = 2^3 \times 7\), and neither 2 nor 7 has that form. \(M\) has to leave remainder 5 on division by 6, so that the fact in the question applies.

node.description: Diagnostic: wrong remainder on division by 6

truefeedback.text: The fact in the question applies only to numbers that leave remainder 5 on division by 6. [[if test='is(rsi < 6)']]If the list were {@tsetstxt[rsi]@}, then \(P = {@tprods[rsi]@}\) and your \(M\) would be {@mvals[rsi]@}, which leaves remainder {@mod(mvals[rsi], 6)@}.[[else]]Your \(M\) does not always leave remainder 5.[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text: Your \(M\) can be divisible by one of the primes in the list. [[if test='is(cpbad = [])']]{@bigp1@} is itself a prime of the form \(6k + 5\), so it would be one of \(p_1, \ldots, p_n\). It would divide \(P\), and so it would divide your \(M\) as well.[[else]][[if test='is(badi < 6)']]If the list were {@tsetstxt[badi]@}, then \(P = {@tprods[badi]@}\) and your \(M\) would be {@mvals[badi]@}, which is divisible by {@badp@}.[[else]]If the list were {@tsetstxt[badi]@}, your \(M\) would be divisible by {@badp@}.[[/if]][[/if]] Then the prime factor of the form \(6k + 5\) could be one of \(p_1, \ldots, p_n\), and there is no contradiction. Compare Euclid's \(N\): dividing it by any listed prime leaves remainder 1.

truefeedback.text: Yes. 5 is one of the primes in the list, and it divides \(6P + 5\), so the prime factor of the form \(6k + 5\) may be 5 itself, and there is no contradiction.
\(6P + 5 = 6 \times P + 5\) does leave remainder 5 on division by 6. Look instead for a prime that divides it.

falsefeedback.text: Look for a prime that divides \(6P + 5\). Is it one of \(p_1, \ldots, p_n\)?
